title: How dental materials behave
blurb: Strength, heat, shrinkage, adhesion and setting: the properties that decide which material the dentist asks for, and how you handle it.
question: The dentist is restoring a deep cavity in a lower molar with amalgam and asks you to mix a lining material first. Afterwards the patient asks why they might feel the cold on their new metal filling. Which material property explains both the lining and the warning?

teach.h: Every material is chosen for how it behaves
teach.body: The mouth is a harsh place. Restorations take heavy biting forces, swing from ice cream to hot tea, sit in saliva and face acid attacks. No single material does everything well, so the dentist picks the one whose properties best suit the job. Your part is to prepare and mix each material exactly as the manufacturer intends, because a badly handled material never reaches the properties it was designed to have.

teach.caption: Exam questions usually describe a clinical problem and ask which property explains it.

head: Property
What it means
Why it matters
rows: Temporaries that wear away lack it
Metals conduct cold to the pulp
Close to tooth = fewer marginal gaps
Silicone impressions can be poured later

teach.body: Enamel and dentine are poor conductors of heat, which protects the pulp. Metals such as amalgam are good conductors, so a deep amalgam can carry cold straight towards the pulp. That is why the dentist places an insulating lining or base underneath. Materials also expand when warm and contract when cold. If a filling expands and contracts much more than the tooth, gaps open at the margins and saliva and bacteria leak in (microleakage). A material whose expansion is close to the tooth's, such as glass ionomer, seals better.

teach.caption: Amalgam relies on mechanical retention from the cavity shape. Composite bonds micromechanically to etched enamel. Glass ionomer bonds chemically to enamel and dentine.

teach.body: Working time runs from the start of mixing until the material can no longer be shaped and placed. Setting time runs from the start of mixing until it has hardened. Heat and extra powder shorten working time; a cool, dry glass slab lengthens it. Many materials keep gaining strength after the initial set, which is why patients are told to avoid biting hard on some new fillings for a while.

steps.label: Start mixing
steps.sub: The clock starts here, not when you hand it over

steps.label: Working time
steps.sub: Place, adapt and shape the material

steps.label: Set and gaining strength
steps.sub: Some materials (e.g. amalgam) take hours to reach full strength

rows.label: Biocompatibility: not harmful to pulp or soft tissue
Low solubility: doesn't dissolve in saliva
Radiopacity: shows up on a radiograph
Translucency: lets light through like enamel
Low film thickness: lets a crown seat fully

teach.note: Radiopacity matters because a restoration that looked dark on a radiograph could be confused with decay.

teach.text: Don't confuse thermal CONDUCTIVITY (how fast heat travels through, the reason for linings under amalgam) with thermal EXPANSION (how much the material changes size, the reason for marginal gaps and leakage).

items: Compressive strength resists biting forces; abrasion resistance resists wear.
Metals conduct heat, so deep amalgams need an insulating lining or base.
Expansion close to the tooth's means fewer marginal gaps and less microleakage.
Composite shrinks as it sets, so it is built up in small increments.
Working time ends before setting time; heat and extra powder shorten both.

summary: You can now name the main property families of dental materials, explain thermal conductivity, thermal expansion, strength, shrinkage, adhesion and working versus setting time, and link each property to what you see chairside: linings under amalgam, increments of composite and temporaries that crack or wear.

A.q: A patient has sensitivity to cold drinks after a large metal restoration was placed. Which property of the metal is most responsible?
A.why: Metals conduct heat well, so cold passes quickly through a metal filling towards the pulp unless it is insulated.

whyNot.0: Low solubility means the material resists dissolving in saliva; it doesn't cause sensitivity.
whyNot.1: Compressive strength is about resisting biting forces, not passing temperature changes.
whyNot.3: Film thickness describes how thin a luting cement spreads under a crown.

A.q: The dentist chooses a material for a core build-up on a molar that will take heavy biting forces. Which property matters most?
A.why: Compressive strength is the ability to resist crushing forces, which is essential under biting load on back teeth.

whyNot.0: Translucency is an aesthetic property, important for front teeth rather than load-bearing cores.
whyNot.2: Fluoride release helps prevent decay but doesn't make a material resist heavy forces.
whyNot.3: Radiopacity lets a material show on a radiograph; it doesn't affect strength.

A.q: Why is composite placed in small increments rather than one large mass?
options: To reduce heat conduction to the pulp
To speed up the setting time
A.why: Composite shrinks as it polymerises. Small increments reduce shrinkage stress at the margins and allow each layer to cure fully.

whyNot.0: Composite already conducts heat poorly; increments don't change that.
whyNot.1: Composite releases little or no fluoride, however it is placed.
whyNot.2: Each increment needs its own curing time, so increments don't make the restoration set faster overall.

B.q: Which statement best describes the working time of a dental material?
options: Time until it reaches its full strength
Time it can be shaped after mixing starts
Time it takes to harden fully in the mouth
Time it can be stored once it is opened
B.why: Working time runs from the start of mixing until the material can no longer be manipulated and placed.

whyNot.0: Reaching full strength can take much longer, sometimes hours, after the material has set.
whyNot.2: That describes setting time, which always ends after working time.
whyNot.3: That describes shelf life after opening, not working time.

B.q: A restorative material expands and contracts with temperature at a rate close to that of natural tooth. What is the main benefit?
options: It no longer needs any bonding
It will never stain or discolour
Fewer marginal gaps and less leakage
It conducts heat more slowly to the pulp
B.why: When filling and tooth change size together, gaps are less likely to open at the margins, reducing microleakage.

whyNot.0: Similar expansion helps the seal but doesn't replace the bonding or retention a material needs.
whyNot.1: Expansion has nothing to do with staining.
whyNot.3: How fast heat passes through is thermal conductivity, a different property.

B.q: A temporary restoration has worn down noticeably within a few weeks. Which property was lacking?
B.why: Abrasion resistance is the ability to resist wear from chewing and brushing. Weak temporary materials wear quickly.

whyNot.1: Biocompatibility is about not harming the tissues, not about wear.
whyNot.2: Dimensional stability describes keeping shape over time, mainly important for impressions.
whyNot.3: Thermal conductivity describes heat transfer, not wear.

C.q: Addition silicone impressions can be poured some time after they are taken, unlike alginate. Which property explains this?
C.why: Addition silicone keeps its shape accurately over time. Alginate loses or gains water and distorts, so it must be poured promptly.

whyNot.0: Compressive strength matters for restorations under biting load, not impression accuracy.
whyNot.1: High thermal expansion would make a material less accurate, not more.
whyNot.2: Solubility in saliva isn't what determines how long an impression stays accurate.

C.q: Which change would SHORTEN the working time of a hand-mixed cement?
options: Mixing on a cool, dry glass slab
C.why: Heat speeds up the setting reaction, so a warm room or slab shortens working time.

whyNot.0: A cool, dry slab slows the reaction and lengthens working time.
whyNot.2: Adding powder in small increments helps control heat and extends working time.
whyNot.3: The correct ratio gives the intended working time; it doesn't shorten it.

C.q: Which property is NOT mainly about how a material looks?
C.why: Radiopacity is about how the material appears on a radiograph, which is a diagnostic property, not an aesthetic one.

whyNot.0: Translucency lets light through like enamel, an aesthetic property.
whyNot.1: Shade stability means the colour doesn't change over time, which is aesthetic.
whyNot.3: Colour match is the most basic aesthetic property of a tooth-coloured material.

reteach.title: Think of a filling like a window frame
reteach.question: A window frame has to survive weather, temperature and years of use. What would make a good frame, and how is a filling the same?

blocks.body: A good window frame is strong enough not to crack (compressive strength) and doesn't wear away (abrasion resistance). A metal frame feels icy in winter because metal conducts cold (thermal conductivity). If the frame swells and shrinks more than the wall, draughts get in round the edges (thermal expansion and leakage). And it needs to be fitted before the filler sets (working time). Fillings face exactly the same tests, only in a mouth instead of a wall.

blocks.text: A question about sensitivity to cold under a metal filling is about conductivity. A question about gaps or leakage at the margins is about expansion or shrinkage.

explain.body: Compressive strength is resistance to crushing, needed wherever teeth bite together: posterior fillings, core build-ups and large temporaries. Abrasion resistance is resistance to wear from chewing and brushing. A temporary that cracks lacks strength; one that wears thin lacks abrasion resistance.

rows.label: Large temporary fractures again and again
Temporary worn flat in two weeks

test.q: A large temporary filling keeps fracturing. Which property should the replacement material have more of?
test.why: Repeated fracture under biting load points to a lack of compressive strength.

whyNot.0: Translucency affects appearance, not resistance to fracture.
whyNot.2: More thermal expansion would worsen the seal, not prevent fracture.
whyNot.3: Higher solubility would make the material dissolve faster, which is worse.

explain.body: Thermal conductivity is how quickly heat passes through a material. Dentine is a natural insulator. Metals conduct heat well, so a deep amalgam needs a lining or base underneath to protect the pulp from hot and cold.

explain.caption: The deeper the cavity, the thinner the insulating dentine left over the pulp, and the more a metal filling needs a lining.

test.q: Why might the dentist place a lining under a deep amalgam?
options: To insulate the pulp from temperature change
To make the amalgam set much more quickly
To help the amalgam bond to the enamel walls
To make the amalgam look more tooth-coloured
test.why: Amalgam conducts heat well, so a lining or base protects the pulp from thermal shock.

whyNot.1: Linings don't change how fast amalgam sets.
whyNot.2: Amalgam is held by mechanical retention, not by a lining bonding it to enamel.
whyNot.3: A lining sits underneath and can't change the colour of the amalgam.

explain.body: All materials change size with temperature. If a filling expands and contracts much more than the tooth, gaps open at the margins and let in saliva and bacteria. Composite also shrinks as it polymerises, so it is placed in small increments to keep the margins sealed.

steps.label: Filling changes size more than tooth

test.q: Which problem is most likely if a filling's thermal expansion is very different from the tooth's?
test.why: Different expansion opens gaps at the margins as temperatures change, allowing microleakage.

whyNot.0: Setting time depends on the setting reaction, not expansion.
whyNot.2: Fluoride release depends on the material's chemistry, not its expansion.
whyNot.3: Radiopacity is about appearance on X-ray, not expansion.

explain.body: Working time is how long you have to mix, hand over and place a material. Setting time is how long it takes to harden. Warmth and too much powder shorten them; a cool, dry slab lengthens working time. Always time from the moment mixing starts.

test.q: When does the working time of a material begin?
options: When it is placed in the cavity
When the dentist asks for it
test.why: Working time is measured from the start of mixing, so delays before handing over eat into it.

whyNot.0: By the time it is placed, some working time has already passed.
whyNot.1: The request starts nothing; the reaction begins when components are mixed.
whyNot.3: Handing over happens after mixing, part-way through the working time.
